I've been a science journalist for fifteen years, and the most important words in any story are the small verbs that nobody notices. When I write that a study shows something, I'm telling you that I believe it. When I write that the authors claim something, I'm keeping my distance. And suggests means that the evidence is interesting, but not yet strong. Most readers never notice the difference, but editors do, and so do the scientists. A few years ago, a headline said that a study proved that coffee helps you live longer. The study proved nothing of the kind. It found that people who drank coffee lived a little longer, which is not the same thing at all. The researchers themselves had warned against reading too much into it. So here is my advice. When you read the news, find the reporting verb first. It tells you how sure the writer is, before you even get to the facts.

I check facts for a magazine, and most of my day is spent on quotes. A writer hands me an article that says, 'The minister admitted that the project was late.' My first question is always the same. Did he admit it, or did he simply say it? Admitted means that he accepted something negative about himself. If he only said it, or explained it, the verb is unfair, and we may get a letter from his lawyer. The same goes for denied, refused and insisted. Each one tells the reader something about the person, not just about the facts. I also check whether a quote is verbatim. If it isn't word for word, we don't use quotation marks. We report it instead. The rule I give young writers is simple. Never choose a verb because it sounds dramatic. Choose the verb that the recording can support. The reporting verb is a very small word, but it's where most of the complaints begin.
